newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nine Japanese feared abducted by N.Korea agents.
newsitem.headline: Nine Japanese feared abducted by N.Korea agents.

text.p: Nine Japanese citizens may have been abducted by North Korean agents and taken to the communist country in the past while two others barely escaped kidnap attempts, the Japanese government said on Friday.

But the government has not yet been able to confirm whether a school girl who went missing 20 years ago was also abducted and taken to North Korea, it said in a statement in response to a query by Lower House legislator Shingo Nishimura.
Japanese media reported earlier in the week that South Korean security officials informed Japan of a North Korean defector's testimony that he knew of a Japanese girl who was abducted 20 years ago.

The description of the girl by the North Korean defector closely resembled the case of Megumi Yokota, then 13, who went missing in 1977 on her way back from school in a coastal village in Niigata Prefecture, central Japan, reports said.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told parliament on Monday the government was investigating the case. But National Police Agency chief Takaji Kunimatsu told reporters on Thursday it may be very difficult to confirm the report.

Friday's statement did not say whether the South Korean government has contacted Japan over the case, or how Tokyo is gathering information, in order to guarantee the privacy and safety of the missing Japanese.
"For the past 20 years we weren't able to do anything because we simply had no idea what had happened to Megumi," her father Shigeru Yokota told a news conference on Friday.

"If it was an abduction, it makes sense we could find no traces of her. At least we can now start to take some action, whether it be to appeal to the Japanese government or the Red Cross or politicians," he said.
Megumi's parents were initially reluctant to reveal their daughter's name to the public, but were persuaded by others that the girl would be safer if her name was revealed.
"If we didn't reveal her name, she may be safe, but we will never be able to see her again," Yokota said.
Reported abductions of Japanese citizens by North Korea have clouded efforts to establish diplomatic relations between the two countries. Tokyo and Seoul established diplomatic ties in 1965.
In 1992, Tokyo and Pyongyang ceased normalisation talks when North Korea rejected Tokyo's demand for information about a Japanese woman it alleged was abducted by North Korean agents.

Kim Hyong-hui, a self-confessed North Korean spy who plotted to blow up a Korean Airlines Boeing 707 in 1987, said Yaeko Taguchi, who went missing in 1978, was the instructor who taught her Japanese language and customs working under the pseudonym Lee Un-hye.
